title: Detail Questions: "According to the Passage"
kicker: American Diploma · ACT · Reading: Key Ideas and Details
summary: How to answer ACT Reading detail questions: locate the line, read around it, and match the paraphrase instead of the exact words.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Detail questions check whether you can **find a specific piece of information in the passage and recognize it when it is said in different words**. They are part of **Key Ideas and Details**, the largest reporting category on ACT Reading (**44–52% of the scored questions**). Detail questions appear with every passage type, and they are usually the fastest points on the test, because the answer is written in the passage. The only skill is finding it and matching it correctly.

rows: "According to the passage, …"
The answer is stated somewhere in the text; you must find where
"The passage states that …" / "The author indicates that …"
Same: a stated fact, almost always paraphrased in the choices
"According to paragraph 4, …" / "In paragraph 2, the narrator says that …"
A paragraph reference: go straight there
"As described in lines 20–25, …" / a quoted phrase in the stem
A line or phrase reference: find the words, then read around them
"The passage indicates that when X happens, Y …"
A detail that is also a relationship: check that the link is the same as in the text

blocks.text: The answer to a detail question is never "what you remember" and never "what is true in real life". It is **what the passage says, in the place the question points to**.
The method: Locate → Read around → Predict → Match

items: **Locate.** If the stem names a paragraph, a line or a quotation, go there. If not, pick a **search word** from the stem: a name, a number, a capitalized word, or an unusual term ("stilts", "learning walk"). Your paragraph labels tell you where to look; then scan for the search word.

**Read around.** Read the sentence before, the sentence with the search word, and the sentence after. Answers are often in the next sentence, especially after a colon or after "however". With a line reference, start a little above the lines and finish a little below them.
**Predict.** Say the answer in a few words of your own: "walked past the nest", "errors add up". This protects you from choices that only sound familiar.

**Match the meaning, not the words.** The correct choice usually paraphrases the text: *walked past* becomes *walked beyond*; *died in the heat* becomes *killed by the heat*. A choice that repeats the passage's exact words is often a trap, because the writers attach those words to the wrong idea.
**Prove it.** Before you choose, put your finger on the sentence that proves your answer. If you cannot, keep looking or eliminate.

blocks.title: المعنى مش الكلمات
blocks.text: في أسئلة According to the passage، الإجابة الصح غالبًا بتقول نفس المعنى بكلمات تانية (paraphrase). أما الاختيار اللي فيه نفس كلمات القطعة بالظبط فخلي بالك منه: كتير بيكون فخ، واخد كلمة من براجراف تاني أو مركّبها على معنى غلط. ارجع للسطر دايمًا، ومتجاوبش من الذاكرة.
How paraphrase works
The test writers change the words of the passage in a few standard ways. If you know them, the right answer jumps out.

rows: "Those on stilts walked past the nest."
✓ They went beyond the nest.
✗ They walked on stilts to the nest. (same words, wrong meaning)
"Small errors add up."
✓ Minor mistakes build up over time.
✗ The ant makes large errors. (changes the size)
"…without satellite signals, which can be blocked by buildings."
✓ They do not depend on signals that buildings may block.
✗ They are blocked by buildings. (reverses who is blocked)
"Some learned from older masters; others taught themselves."
✓ Their training varied.
✗ All were trained by older masters. (some → all)
"The fridge was removed within a year."
✓ It lasted less than a year.
✗ It was removed after several years. (changes the number)

blocks.text: Notice what the traps change: **who** does something, **how much** (some/all, small/large), **when**, or **which way** the relationship goes. One changed word is enough to make a choice wrong.
Line and paragraph references

items: **A paragraph reference limits the search, not the answer's words.** The answer still paraphrases the sentence; it does not copy it.
**The answer may be just outside the lines.** A quoted phrase is often explained in the next sentence. Always read one sentence further.

**Wrong-place traps.** Choices often contain facts that ARE in the passage, but in a different paragraph. True + wrong place = wrong answer. ✗ In the ant passage, "recognizes stones near the nest" is true, but it is not what path integration does.

**Two groups, swapped.** When a passage describes two groups (long legs and short legs, before and after, supporters and critics), a trap gives one group's result to the other. Underline which result belongs to which group.

blocks.text: Worked examples
Read this short natural science excerpt (shorter than a real ACT passage, so we can focus on the method). Then study each question.

[1] Sea turtles lay their eggs in sandy nests on beaches, and about two months later the hatchlings dig their way to the surface, usually at night. They then face the most dangerous journey of their lives: a crawl of a few meters, sometimes much more, across open sand to the water.

[2] For a long time it was assumed that the young turtles found the sea by smell or by the sound of the waves. Experiments showed otherwise. Hatchlings move toward the brightest, lowest part of the horizon, which on a natural beach is almost always the open sea, where light from the moon and stars reflects off the water. Dark, tall shapes such as dunes and vegetation, which usually lie inland, push them in the opposite direction.

[3] This guidance system worked well for millions of years. Along brightly lit coasts today, however, the brightest horizon may be a hotel or a road. Hatchlings that crawl toward these lights can die of exhaustion, be caught by predators or be crushed by traffic. Some coastal towns now require shielded lights or switch off beach lighting during the nesting season.
**Worked example 1 — "According to the passage"**
**Question:** According to the passage, hatchlings on a natural beach find the sea by:

items: A) following the smell of salt water.
B) listening for the sound of the waves.
C) heading toward the brightest, lowest part of the horizon.
D) following the adult turtles back to the water.

blocks.text: **Answer: C.** Search word: "find the sea" → paragraph 2. Read around: "Experiments showed otherwise. Hatchlings move toward the brightest, lowest part of the horizon." C paraphrases this.

items: **A is wrong** — Words from the passage, wrong meaning: smell was what people ASSUMED, and "experiments showed otherwise."
**B is wrong** — Same trap: the sound of the waves is the rejected idea. Reading only one sentence would catch you.
**D is wrong** — Outside knowledge: adult turtles are never mentioned.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — paragraph reference**
**Question:** According to paragraph 2, dunes and vegetation affect hatchlings by:

items: A) reflecting light from the moon and stars.
B) hiding the hatchlings from predators.
C) making the hatchlings crawl faster.
D) steering the hatchlings away from the land.

blocks.text: **Answer: D.** "Dark, tall shapes such as dunes and vegetation … push them in the opposite direction" — opposite to the dark, inland shapes means toward the sea, away from the land. D is the paraphrase.

items: **A is wrong** — Wrong relationship: the reflection belongs to the sea, not to the dunes.
**B is wrong** — Predators appear in paragraph 3 and are linked to artificial lights, not to dunes.
**C is wrong** — Not stated: speed is never discussed.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — detail from a list**
**Question:** The passage states that some coastal towns have responded to the problem of artificial light by:

items: A) banning hotels near nesting beaches.
B) shielding lights or switching off beach lighting in the nesting season.
C) moving turtle nests to dark beaches.
D) switching off all the lights in the town at night.

blocks.text: **Answer: B.** Last sentence: "require shielded lights or switch off beach lighting during the nesting season." B keeps both parts and the time limit.

items: **A is wrong** — Too extreme and invented: hotels are named as a light source, not banned.
**C is wrong** — Outside knowledge: sounds sensible, but the passage never says it.
**D is wrong** — Exact words, changed size: the text says BEACH lighting during the nesting SEASON, not all lights in the town.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — cause in a detail question**
**Question:** According to the passage, hatchlings on brightly lit coasts are in danger because they:

items: A) crawl toward lights on land instead of toward the sea.
B) cannot see the dunes in the bright light.
C) hatch during the day instead of at night.
D) are attracted by the noise of traffic.

blocks.text: **Answer: A.** Paragraph 3: "the brightest horizon may be a hotel or a road", and hatchlings that "crawl toward these lights" die. A states the cause the passage gives.

items: **B is wrong** — Invented: nothing says light hides the dunes.
**C is wrong** — Contradicted: hatchlings come out "usually at night"; nothing says lighting changes this.
**D is wrong** — Wrong relationship: traffic is a danger they meet, not what attracts them.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Answering from memory.** Your memory of a 700-word passage blurs details. Go back to the line every time.
**Same words, wrong meaning.** The choice repeats the text's exact words but attaches them to the wrong person, group or idea.
**Wrong place.** A true fact from another paragraph. True is not enough; it must answer THIS question.
**The rejected idea.** Passages often state an old belief and then correct it ("It was assumed… Experiments showed otherwise"). The old belief is a favourite trap.
**Changed amount.** some → all, several → most, beach lighting → all lighting, a few meters → far away.
**Swapped groups.** Two groups with different results (long legs / short legs); the trap gives one group's result to the other.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Do paragraph- and line-reference detail questions first: they are the quickest points in the set.
Choose a search word from the stem; use your paragraph labels to find it.
Read the sentence before, the sentence and the sentence after.
Predict in a few words, then pick the PARAPHRASE of your prediction.
Put your finger on the proof sentence before you click.

blocks.title: لو السؤال فيه رقم براجراف
blocks.text: روح على البراجراف ده على طول، واقرا جملة قبل الكلمة وجملة بعدها. لو في مجموعتين في القطعة (زي النمل اللي رجليه طويلة والنمل اللي رجليه قصيرة)، حدد نتيجة كل مجموعة كويس، لأن الفخ المشهور إنهم يبدلوا النتايج.
Practice

Now try a full natural science passage (about 720 words) with 9 questions, almost all of them detail questions. It is **untimed**, but aim for about 10 minutes. Locate, read around, predict, and match the paraphrase.

blocks.title: ACT Reading practice — Detail questions (Natural Science)
blocks.intro: One passage, 9 questions, untimed. For every question, find the proof sentence before you answer. Watch for exact-word traps, wrong-place traps and swapped groups.

questions.p:
NATURAL SCIENCE: This passage is adapted from an article about how desert ants find their way home.

[1] At midday on the salt flats of North Africa, the ground can become hot enough to kill most insects within minutes. Yet this is exactly when certain desert ants of the genus Cataglyphis leave their nests to hunt. They search for insects that have died in the heat, and each forager must find its prey, grab it and get back underground before its own body overheats. An ant may wander more than a hundred meters from the nest on a twisting outward route, but once it has found food, it turns and runs home in a nearly straight line. For decades, biologists have tried to explain how an animal with a brain far smaller than a pinhead performs this feat.

[2] The answer, it turns out, is not a single sense but a combination of systems. The most important is known as path integration. As the ant moves, it keeps continuous track of two things: the direction in which it is travelling and the distance it has covered. By combining these measurements at every moment, it always has an estimate of the straight-line direction and distance back to the nest, even though it cannot see the nest itself. Sailors before the age of satellite navigation did something similar, working out their position from their compass heading, their speed and the time that had passed. They called the method dead reckoning.

[3] To measure direction, the ant uses the sky. Sunlight scattered by the atmosphere becomes polarized, forming a pattern across the sky that depends on the position of the sun. Specialized cells in the upper part of the ant's eyes detect this pattern, which gives the insect a compass even when the sun itself is hidden from part of its view. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, the ant must also allow for the time; researchers believe it does so, although exactly how is still being studied.

[4] Distance was the harder puzzle. In a well-known series of experiments, researchers trained ants to walk from their nest to a feeder along a straight channel. Once the ants had reached the feeder, the scientists changed the length of their legs: some ants had tiny extensions, often described as stilts, attached to their legs, while others had their legs carefully shortened. The ants were then released to walk home. Those on stilts walked past the nest, while those with shorter legs stopped before reaching it. The result suggested that the ants measure distance by, in effect, counting their steps: longer legs meant longer steps, so the usual number of steps carried them too far.

[5] Path integration has a weakness, however: small errors add up. Every slight mistake in measuring a turn or a step is carried forward, so that after a long journey the ant's estimate may be off by several meters. For a creature looking for a nest entrance only a few millimeters wide, that is a serious problem. Here a second system helps. Near the nest, the ants learn the appearance of nearby landmarks, such as stones or small plants, and use them to guide the final part of the journey. Ants that leave the nest for the first time often perform short "learning walks," stopping and turning to face the entrance as if memorizing the view.

[6] When both systems fail, the ant has a backup plan. If it reaches the spot where path integration says the nest should be and finds nothing, it begins a systematic search, walking in loops of increasing size centered on that spot. Because the loops keep returning to the starting point, the ant spends most of its searching time close to where the nest is most likely to be.

[7] Researchers have also found that the ants use smells carried by the wind near the nest, especially where the ground offers few visual clues. Others are interested in what the ants can teach engineers. Small robots that combine a polarized-light compass with step counting have already been built and tested, and they can navigate without satellite signals, which can be blocked by buildings or interrupted. The ant, which cannot afford to lose its way for even a few minutes in the midday heat, has turned out to be an excellent teacher.
questions.q: According to paragraph 1, Cataglyphis ants leave the nest at midday in order to look for:
c: cooler ground where they can rest.
landmarks that will guide them home.
insects that have been killed by the heat.
a new site for their nest.
questions.e: "They search for insects that have died in the heat." C is a paraphrase (died in the heat = killed by the heat). A is reversed (the ground is dangerously hot); B belongs to paragraph 5 and is not why they leave; D is never mentioned.

questions.q: According to the passage, path integration allows an ant to:
c: keep an estimate of the direction and distance back to its nest without seeing the nest.
retrace its twisting outward route exactly, step by step.
recognize stones and small plants close to the nest entrance.
detect smells carried by the wind from the nest.
questions.e: Paragraph 2: by combining direction and distance, the ant "always has an estimate of the straight-line direction and distance back to the nest, even though it cannot see the nest." B is contradicted (it runs home in a straight line, not along the outward route). C is the landmark system (paragraph 5); D is smell (paragraph 7) — true details from the wrong place.

questions.q: The passage states that the ant's sky compass works by detecting:
c: the exact position of the sun at every moment.
the Earth's magnetic field.
the shadows cast by stones near the nest.

questions.e: Paragraph 3: cells in the ant's eyes "detect this pattern" of polarized light, which works "even when the sun itself is hidden from part of its view." A misses that point. B is outside knowledge — never mentioned. C mixes in landmarks from paragraph 5.

questions.q: According to paragraph 4, when ants with lengthened legs were released to walk home, they:
c: stopped before they reached the nest.
walked beyond the nest.

questions.q: According to the passage, the main weakness of path integration is that:
c: it works only when the sun is clearly visible.
small measuring errors build up over a long journey.
young ants must learn it during their first walks.
it cannot measure distance, only direction.
questions.e: Paragraph 5: "small errors add up … after a long journey the ant's estimate may be off by several meters." questions.q: According to paragraph 5, during a "learning walk" an ant:
c: counts the number of steps between landmarks.
follows an older ant back to the nest.
stops and turns to face the nest entrance.
carries food back to the nest for the first time.
questions.e: "stopping and turning to face the entrance as if memorizing the view." C matches. A blends paragraph 4 (steps) with paragraph 5 (landmarks). B and D are never stated.

questions.q: The passage indicates that if an ant arrives where it expects the nest to be and does not find it, the ant:
c: searches in widening loops that keep returning to that spot.
goes back to the place where it found its food and starts again.
waits in that spot until other ants appear.
walks in a straight line until it sees a familiar landmark.
questions.e: Paragraph 6: it walks "in loops of increasing size centered on that spot" that "keep returning to the starting point." A paraphrases this. B, C and D are invented behaviours; D also contradicts the loop pattern.

questions.q: According to paragraph 7, robots built on the ants' methods are useful because they:
c: can carry heavier loads than insect-sized machines.
use smell to find their way when the ground is dark.
are cheaper to build than robots with cameras.
can find their way without satellite signals.
questions.e: The robots "can navigate without satellite signals, which can be blocked by buildings or interrupted." D matches. B takes the word "smells" from the first sentence of the paragraph but attaches it to the robots (wrong relationship). A and C are never mentioned.

questions.q: Based on the passage, it can most reasonably be inferred that an ant relying on path integration alone after a very long journey would most likely:
c: arrive at the exact nest entrance without difficulty.
be unable to choose any direction at all.
arrive near the nest but possibly miss its small entrance.
return along its outward route to correct its errors.
questions.e: Paragraph 5 says errors build up and the estimate "may be off by several meters," which is "a serious problem" for an entrance a few millimeters wide. One small step: it would get close but might miss the entrance. A ignores the weakness. B is too extreme: it still has an estimate. D is not supported (and contradicts the straight-line return).

items: Detail questions ("According to the passage…") are part of Key Ideas and Details, 44–52% of scored ACT Reading questions.
Locate → read around (sentence before and after) → predict → match.
The right answer paraphrases the text; a choice with the exact words is often a trap.
True but in the wrong paragraph is still wrong.
Never answer from memory: prove every answer with a sentence.
